metadata.query_source: I'm trying to scope out my research proposal. It's focused on decentralized control for a heterogeneous swarm (UAVs and UGVs) doing search and rescue in unstructured, GPS-denied environments. Think collapsed buildings, dense forests, etc First, I need a way for each agent to handle its own state estimation. I'm thinking multi-sensor fusion, that is, fusing onboard vision, LiDAR, and IMU data for robust SLAM and odometry, but it also has to be good enough to detect survivors or hazards, not just navigate. How do we manage real-time role assignment, eg who's mapping, who's actively searching, who's clearing debris? It needs to be decentralized and robust to failures. for example if a drone battery dies or a ground bot gets stuck, the system has to autonomously reallocate its tasks without a central coordinator. The comms will be spotty, so how does the swarm propagate critical info like victim locations, new hazards, blocked passages, etc over an ad-hoc mesh network that's constantly dropping connections? Maybe some distributed mapping or data sharing protocol? For the analysis, I need to show this framework is actually effective. We probably need some formal or at least strong empirical guarantees? Something to show that, say 90% of reachable victims are located within a bounded time, even if we lose up to 30% of the agents. Finally, for evaluation, I'm planning to implement this in a high-fidelity simulator, probably ROS/Gazebo, with realistic sensor noise and complex terrain. Then I'd run it across maybe three disaster scenarios of increasing complexity. We'd need to report metrics on coverage, victim-finding rate, rescue latency, and the network overhead to make sure it's efficient.

An off-board ground station fuses individual maps from multiple drones into a global 3-D map that can be monitored by human rescuers.

In a real-world implementation, though not in the current system, the drones would come equipped with object detection to identify a missing hiker. When located, the drone would tag the hiker's location on the global map. Humans could then use this information to plan a rescue mission.

How, the Richard Cockburn Maclaurin Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics.

Exploring and mapping

On each drone, the researchers mounted a LIDAR system, which creates a 2-D scan of the surrounding obstacles by shooting laser beams and measuring the reflected pulses. This can be used to detect trees; however, to drones, individual trees appear remarkably similar. If a drone can't recognize a given tree, it can't determine if it's already explored an area.

The researchers programmed their drones to instead identify multiple trees' orientations, which is far more distinctive. With this method, when the LIDAR signal returns a cluster of trees, an algorithm calculates the angles and distances between trees to identify that cluster. "Drones can use that as a unique signature to tell if they've visited this area before or if it's a new area," Tian says.

This feature-detection technique helps the ground station accurately merge maps. The drones generally explore an area in loops, producing scans as they go. The ground station continuously monitors the scans. When two drones loop around to the same cluster of trees, the ground station merges the maps by calculating the relative transformation between the drones, and then fusing the individual maps to maintain consistent orientations.

"Calculating that relative transformation tells you how you should align the two maps so it corresponds to exactly how the forest looks," Tian says.

Unexplored areas are dark but turn gray as they're mapped by a drone. On-board path-planning software tells a drone to always explore these dark unexplored areas as it flies around. Producing a 3-D map is more reliable than simply attaching a camera to a drone and monitoring the video feed, Tian says. Transmitting video to a central station, for instance, requires a lot of bandwidth that may not be available in forested areas.

More efficient searching

A key innovation is a novel search strategy that let the drones more efficiently explore an area. According to a more traditional approach, a drone would always search the closest possible unknown area. However, that could be in any number of directions from the drone's current position. The drone usually flies a short distance, and then stops to select a new direction.

"That doesn't respect dynamics of drone [movement]," Tian says. "It has to stop and turn, so that means it's very inefficient in terms of time and energy, and you can't really pick up speed."

Instead, the researchers' drones explore the closest possible area, while considering their current direction. They believe this can help the drones maintain a more consistent velocity. This strategy — where the drone tends to travel in a spiral pattern — covers a search area much faster. "In search and rescue missions, time is very important," Tian says.

In the future, they hope to design the drones to communicate wirelessly when approaching one another, fuse their maps, and then cut communication when they separate. The ground station, in that case, would only be used to monitor the updated global map.

A group of autonomous mobile robots with limited sensing

Robots complete the task in a distributed and non-centralized

Finding or nonexistent in forest environments.

In a paper being presented at the International Symposium on Experimental Robotics conference next week, MIT researchers describe an autonomous system for a fleet of drones to collaboratively search under dense forest canopies. The drones use only onboard computation and wireless communication — no GPS required.

Each autonomous quadrotor drone is equipped with laser-range finders for position estimation, localization, and path planning. As the drone flies around, it creates an individual 3-D map of the terrain. Algorithms help it recognize unexplored and already-searched spots, so it knows when it's fully mapped an area. An off-board ground station fuses individual maps from multiple drones into a global 3-D map that can be monitored by human rescuers.

In a real-world implementation, though not in the current system, the drones would come equipped with object detection to identify a missing hiker. When located, the drone would tag the hiker's location on the global map. Humans could then use this information to plan a rescue mission.

"Essentially, we're replacing humans with a fleet of drones to make the search part of the search-and-rescue process more efficient," says first author Yulun Tian, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro).

The researchers tested multiple drones in simulations of randomly generated forests, and tested two drones in a forested area within NASA's Langley Research Center. In both experiments, each drone mapped a roughly 20-square-meter area in about two to five minutes and collaboratively fused their maps together in real-time. The drones also performed well across several metrics, including overall speed and time to complete the mission, detection of forest features, and accurate merging of maps.

Co-authors on the paper are: Katherine Liu, a PhD student in MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) and AeroAstro; Kyel Ok, a PhD student in CSAIL and the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science; Loc Tran and Danette Allen of the NASA Langley Research Center; Nicholas Roy, an AeroAstro professor and CSAIL researcher; and Jonathan P. How, the Richard Cockburn Maclaurin Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics.

On each drone, the researchers mounted a LIDAR system, which creates a 2-D scan of the surrounding obstacles by shooting laser beams and measuring the reflected pulses. According to a more traditional approach, a drone would always search the closest possible unknown area. However, that could be in any number of directions from the drone's current position. A strong proposal would frame the system as a decentralized, failure-aware, heterogeneous autonomy stack rather than as a single swarm controller.

Each UAV and UGV should maintain its own local state estimate, local metric-semantic map, detected-object database, task state, and estimate of neighbouring agents without depending on a central coordinator. [shard_05646_60097] [shard_04181_27198]

For state estimation, use a tightly coupled visual–LiDAR–IMU estimator in which IMU data provide high-rate motion propagation, LiDAR constrains geometric drift in texture-poor or dark environments, and camera measurements provide visual features and semantic observations. [shard_03511_47557] [shard_04397_75063]

A factor-graph or sliding-window formulation is preferable because it can represent asynchronous measurements, loop closures, inter-robot observations, and delayed relative-pose constraints, while a robust loss function can reduce the effect of bad visual matches, dust, smoke, dynamic objects, and LiDAR outliers.

The estimator should publish both a pose and uncertainty, because role assignment and navigation should penalize agents whose localization confidence has degraded rather than treating every pose estimate as equally reliable.

Perception should be split into navigation and mission layers, with the first producing free space, traversability, obstacles, and localization features, and the second producing survivor, fire, smoke, gas, structural-damage, and blockage hypotheses. [shard_00918_74993] [shard_02921_6069]

Camera, LiDAR, and thermal or audio sensing should be treated as complementary rather than interchangeable, since cameras support recognition, LiDAR supports geometry and illumination-independent ranging, and thermal or audio sensing can provide additional survivor evidence in collapsed structures. [shard_03511_47557] [shard_02921_6069]

Each detection should be stored as a probabilistic semantic landmark containing its class, position and covariance, confidence, timestamp, observing agent, supporting sensor modalities, and status such as unverified, confirmed, rescued, or obsolete.

The shared world model should use submaps and semantic event records instead of continuously transmitting raw point clouds or video, because a prior GPS-denied multi-drone system demonstrated real-time map fusion but still depended on an off-board station and a wireless router for map merging. [shard_05646_60097]

The decentralized mapping layer can exchange compressed submap summaries, loop-closure candidates, frontier descriptors, traversability changes, and semantic events whenever agents encounter one another, using peer-to-peer map fusion rather than a permanent global server. [shard_04181_27198] [shard_02023_14078]

A useful communication protocol is store-carry-forward gossip with anti-entropy synchronization, where every message has a unique identifier, sequence number, time-to-live, priority, confidence, and geographic or topological scope.

Victim locations, imminent hazards, and newly blocked passages should receive highest priority and should be replicated redundantly across available neighbours, whereas detailed imagery and redundant map data should be opportunistically transmitted when bandwidth permits.

The protocol must explicitly represent uncertainty and conflict, so two agents reporting different locations for the same survivor produce a track-merging problem rather than an unsafe overwrite.

This approach is appropriate for an intermittently connected mesh because ad-hoc networks operate without fixed infrastructure or central administration, but their changing topology makes delivery and bounded dissemination nontrivial. [shard_01529_28218] [shard_06155_6794] [shard_03256_4170]

Role assignment should be formulated as a rolling decentralized task-allocation problem over tasks such as frontier mapping, active survivor search, hazard verification, debris inspection, relay placement, victim tracking, and rescue support.

Every agent should compute bids from capability compatibility, distance, energy reserve, localization uncertainty, expected information gain, risk, communication connectivity, and the marginal effect of leaving its current task.

A lightweight market or consensus mechanism can assign tasks locally, with leases, expiration times, and explicit relinquishment messages so that a task becomes available automatically when an agent dies, becomes stuck, loses energy, or fails a health check. [shard_00267_19082] [shard_04973_285]

The allocation objective should include minimum capability requirements, redundancy for critical tasks, and graceful degradation, since heterogeneous-resilience methods explicitly reallocate agents when environmental conditions degrade particular capabilities. [shard_02654_73087]

For example, a UAV can receive a high bid for rapid aerial mapping and relay placement, a UGV can receive a high bid for traversable-ground search or debris interaction, and either platform can bid for survivor verification if it possesses the necessary sensors.

The allocation algorithm should be compared against at least a greedy nearest-task baseline, a static role assignment, and a centralized oracle, since rescue-specific studies report that local-information mechanisms such as Swarm-GAP and LA-DCOP can outperform greedy allocation without explicit negotiation. [shard_02703_17618]

The central research hypothesis could be that event-driven local allocation plus replicated semantic information maintains mission performance under agent loss and intermittent connectivity better than static roles or raw-data sharing.

The proposed guarantee should be stated conditionally rather than as an unconditional promise that 90 percent of victims will always be found after losing 30 percent of the swarm.

Define a reachable victim as one lying in the traversable or sensor-accessible region under the scenario’s motion, sensing, and battery model, and define detection time as the interval from mission start or victim exposure to the first detection that passes a specified confidence threshold.

Then test the claim that, for a specified scenario distribution, at least 90 percent of reachable victims are detected within time T with at least 95 percent confidence when up to 30 percent of agents fail, while separately reporting the probability of communication partition and the fraction of victims outside the surviving team’s sensing capacity.

This distinction is essential because no algorithm can guarantee a fixed victim-recovery percentage under arbitrary simultaneous failures, permanent network partitions, inaccessible victims, or insufficient remaining sensing and mobility resources.

The simulator should be implemented as a reproducible ROS/Gazebo experiment with heterogeneous UAV and UGV dynamics, realistic camera, LiDAR, IMU, thermal or audio models, battery depletion, collision risk, terrain-dependent radio propagation, packet loss, latency, and agent failures. [shard_02319_71674]

The three scenarios should increase in difficulty from a dense forest with limited GPS and moderate occlusion, to a collapsed urban structure with narrow passages and debris, and finally to a mixed disaster containing smoke, fire, blocked routes, uneven terrain, intermittent connectivity, and heterogeneous victim and hazard types. [shard_05646_60097] [shard_03273_54009]

Each scenario should include fixed victim ground truth, reachable-region annotations, hazard locations, terrain maps, communication traces, and repeated randomized seeds so that detection and coverage results are statistically comparable.

The primary metrics should be reachable-area coverage over time, victim-finding precision and recall, time to first detection, time to confirmed location, rescue or handoff latency, hazard-detection recall, localization error, map consistency, task-reallocation latency, mission completion rate, surviving-agent utilization, packet delivery ratio, end-to-end alert latency, bytes transmitted per detected victim, and energy consumed per square metre covered. [shard_04695_31460] [shard_02023_14078]

Ablation studies should independently remove LiDAR, visual sensing, semantic event sharing, peer-to-peer map fusion, failure-aware bidding, and message prioritization to identify which components produce the claimed robustness.

The final evaluation should report medians, 90th and 95th percentiles, confidence intervals, and failure distributions rather than only average performance, with comparisons across zero, 10, 20, and 30 percent agent loss and across connected, intermittent, and partitioned communication conditions.

The proposal’s defensible contribution is therefore a decentralized architecture that couples uncertainty-aware multimodal estimation, semantic submap exchange, lease-based heterogeneous task allocation, and priority-aware delay-tolerant networking, validated by conditional probabilistic guarantees and controlled simulation experiments rather than by an unsupported universal guarantee.

A strong proposal should frame the system as a decentralized, failure-aware autonomy stack rather than as a single swarm controller.

A factor-graph or sliding-window estimator is suitable because it can represent asynchronous measurements, loop closures, inter-robot observations, and delayed relative-pose constraints, while robust loss functions can reduce the influence of bad visual matches and LiDAR outliers.

The estimator should publish both a pose and uncertainty, because navigation and task allocation should penalize agents whose localization confidence has degraded rather than treating every estimate as equally reliable.

Perception should be divided into navigation and mission layers, with the first producing free space, traversability, obstacles, and localization features, and the second producing survivor, fire, smoke, structural-damage, and blockage hypotheses. [shard_00918_74993] [shard_02921_6069]

Camera, LiDAR, and thermal or audio sensing should be treated as complementary, since cameras support recognition, LiDAR supports geometry and illumination-independent ranging, and thermal or audio sensing can provide additional survivor evidence in collapsed structures. Each detection should be represented as a probabilistic semantic landmark containing its class, position and covariance, confidence, timestamp, observing agent, supporting modalities, and status such as unverified, confirmed, rescued, or obsolete.

The shared world model should exchange compressed submap summaries, loop-closure candidates, frontier descriptors, traversability changes, and semantic events rather than continuously transmitting raw point clouds or video, because a GPS-denied multi-drone system demonstrated real-time map fusion but still depended on an off-board station and wireless router for merging. The mapping layer can use peer-to-peer submap fusion whenever agents encounter one another, with store-carry-forward gossip and anti-entropy synchronization for disconnected periods. [shard_04181_27198] [shard_02023_14078]

Every message should have a unique identifier, sequence number, time-to-live, priority, confidence, and geographic or topological scope.

Victim locations, imminent hazards, and newly blocked passages should be replicated redundantly across available neighbours, while detailed imagery and redundant map data should be transmitted opportunistically.

The protocol must represent uncertainty and conflict, so two reports about one survivor produce a track-merging problem rather than an unsafe overwrite.

Each agent should compute bids from capability compatibility, distance, energy reserve, localization uncertainty, expected information gain, risk, communication connectivity, and the marginal effect of leaving its current task.

A market or consensus mechanism can assign tasks locally, using leases, expiration times, and relinquishment messages so that a task becomes available when an agent dies, becomes stuck, loses energy, or fails a health check. [shard_00267_19082] [shard_04973_285]
